title: One Hand or Two? What Changes in a Loaded Carry
subtitle: Farmer carries and suitcase carries look simple, but they ask your body to manage weight in different ways. Here’s how to compare them without turning the exercise into a test.
imageAlt: Two friends walk side by side along a clear indoor path, each carrying a comfortable weight: one holds a weight in each hand, the other carries one weight at their side.
imageConcept: A warm, natural-light scene with two friends on a clear, flat indoor route. One demonstrates a farmer carry with a manageable weight in each hand; the other demonstrates a suitcase carry with one weight, held comfortably at their side. They move at their own pace, with relaxed expressions and no competition or matching loads.
body: The same walk, a different challenge

A loaded carry is exactly what it sounds like: pick up a weight and walk with it under control. In a farmer carry, you hold a load in each hand. In a suitcase carry, you hold one load at one side. Both involve grip and walking, but the load is distributed differently, so your body has different demands to manage.

That difference is useful to understand—and easy to oversell. A suitcase carry may feel more challenging because the load is off-center. That sensation does not make it automatically better, more effective, or more suitable for everyone. The practical question is not which version wins, but what you want to practice and what you can do comfortably.
What the research can—and cannot—tell us

A small study of 18 healthy, college-aged participants measured muscle activity during different carries, holds and planks. The carry variations produced different muscle-activation patterns. That’s evidence that the movements are not identical; it is not proof that one builds more strength over time or is best for a general reader. Short-term muscle-activity measurements cannot settle those questions. [1]

A separate biomechanics study had six participants walk with buckets while researchers modeled spinal loading. Under the specific conditions tested, the model estimated more low-back loading when a load was carried in one hand than when it was divided between both hands. This does not show that suitcase carries cause injury, nor does it establish a universal ranking for training. It is a small study of modeled loads, not a long-term injury trial. [2]

The distinction matters: a movement can place different demands on the body without being inherently unsafe or superior. The evidence here is specific and limited; let it inform curiosity, not dictate a verdict.
A carry is an option, not a whole program

Carrying can be a practical part of strength training, especially when the load is substantial enough to require effort and the activity involves major muscle groups. U.S. physical activity guidance includes carrying heavy loads among examples of muscle-strengthening activity, while also emphasizing variety. [3]

That broader context is more useful than treating carries as a complete workout. A balanced strength practice can include different movements and ways of working the major muscle groups; carries are one possible ingredient. You do not need to add them because an exercise is trendy, or use them to prove that ordinary tasks are easy. If you enjoy the simple challenge of moving a load with control, they may have a place. If they do not suit your space, equipment, body or preferences, other strength exercises can serve you too.
Choose the version for the job

A farmer carry keeps the weight balanced from side to side, provided the loads are similar. It can be a straightforward way to practice holding and walking with weight. A suitcase carry places the weight on one side, so you have to manage an asymmetrical load as you move. That may be useful if you want to explore that particular challenge, but “harder to stabilize” is not a synonym for “better.”

Your choice can be simple. If you are learning the movement, prefer the more balanced feel, or have only a pair of manageable objects, start with the farmer carry. If you already find carrying comfortable and want to try an off-center load, test the suitcase version with a lighter or otherwise easy-to-control weight. You can also choose neither on a given day. Comfort, control and context are better guides than a rule that one variation is mandatory.
A low-pressure way to compare them

Try this as a movement check, not a workout prescription or a maximum-load test. Use stable weights you can pick up and set down with control, and choose a clear, flat route without pets, loose rugs or obstacles. Wear shoes that feel secure, and leave enough room to turn without rushing.

First, pick up one weight and walk a short, comfortable stretch. Set it down gently. Notice whether you can keep a steady pace, whether your grip feels secure, and whether the route gives you room to move naturally. If you have a matched pair of weights, repeat the walk holding one in each hand. Keep the loads manageable; there is no need to match the total weight across variations or make the comparison mathematically exact.

If you try the suitcase carry, you can switch sides on a later pass rather than rushing to change hands mid-walk. Notice whether the two sides feel different, without assuming they must feel identical. Stop if you cannot control the weight, your grip is failing, or you feel pain, dizziness or unusual symptoms. If you have a health condition, a recent injury or uncertainty about whether loaded exercise is appropriate, seek individualized guidance from a qualified health professional.

A useful comparison is not a contest over who carried more, walked farther or looked more athletic. Pay attention to a few practical details: Was the pickup controlled? Could you take smooth steps? Did the weight feel manageable in your hand? Could you set it down without dropping or twisting in a hurry? Those observations can help you decide whether to repeat the movement, adjust the setup or choose another exercise.

The science on loaded carries is still narrow. The available studies do not establish a universally best carry, an ideal home load or a proven injury-prevention effect. [1] and [2] help explain why the two patterns differ; they do not answer every training question.

That leaves room for sound judgment. Choose a version that fits your goal and setting; use a load you can handle without strain; and make changes gradually if you choose to include carries in a broader strength routine. You might use both variations at different times, or stick with one because it feels more practical. The point is not to find the hardest-looking option. It is to practice a movement that is useful to you, with enough control to repeat it.
